UX Case Study — 2026

PalUp

Finding your next meal companion —
one conversation at a time.

A mobile app that connects people for shared dining experiences in a new city, built from research through high-fidelity prototype.

Role

UX Researcher & Interaction Designer

Timeline

January – April 2026

Team

Siyu Ai · Karena Ma · Suiyang Mai · Xinran Wang

Tools

Figma · Affinity Diagrams · Interviews

01 — The Problem

Moving to a new city means eating alone — a lot.

Communal dishes like hotpot and dim sum lose their appeal without company. Existing platforms like Meetup handle large events, but nothing exists for the simple, recurring need: finding one to three people to share a meal with.

We set out to design a mobile app that makes it effortless to find a compatible dining companion — not just someone who likes the same cuisine, but someone you can actually talk to.

"People don't want a dining companion who likes the same food. They want someone they can actually talk to."

Core insight from user research

02 — Research

How we learned what users actually need

8 semi-structured interviews with Chinese immigrants living in Seattle (1–10 years in the US). Sessions were in-person and via Zoom. Participants lived alone or had limited social networks.

Theme 1

Conversation > Cuisine

Conversational fit was prioritized over food preferences when evaluating potential dining companions — consistently across all participants.

Theme 2

Group Size Matters

4 people was cited as ideal — small enough to talk meaningfully, large enough to reduce awkward silences.

Theme 3

Safety Is a Prerequisite

Trust mechanisms were non-negotiable for female participants — safety was expected, not a bonus feature.

Theme 4

The Bad Cycle

Fewer friends → less dining out → harder to meet people. A self-reinforcing isolation loop the app needed to break.

User Persona

Angela Zhang

28 · Software Engineer · Seattle. Loves communal dining, struggles to find compatible companions without it feeling like a date. Represents our core user: recently relocated, independent, socially motivated but constrained.

03 — Design Process

Four iterative phases

Each phase built directly on what we learned. Every design decision traced back to a specific finding from research or evaluation.

01

Phase 01

Paper Prototype

We sketched four core task flows — managing a profile, finding and joining an event, creating an event, and chatting with participants. Each team member owned one flow and we produced rough paper prototypes for a cross-team heuristic evaluation.

The evaluation surfaced 12 issues. Three were rated most severe:

Severe issues found

  • → No send button visible in the chat interface
  • → No way to leave a chatroom once joined
  • → Event creation and home browsing shared the same screen — users couldn't distinguish which mode they were in

Before heuristic evaluation

After heuristic evaluation — revised paper prototypes

02

Phase 02

Wireframes — Low Fidelity

We moved into Figma and connected all four flows into a single interactive prototype, applying every fix from the heuristic evaluation.

Key changes

  • → Added floating "+" button as dedicated event creation trigger
  • → Added error states to the login flow
  • → Separated browsing and creating into distinct screens

Heuristic evaluation — issues annotated on screens

03

Phase 03

Medium-Fidelity Prototype

User testing with 4–5 participants revealed two persistent issues in the Create Event flow that had survived from the wireframe stage.

Issue 1

Newly posted events weren't tappable on Home

Users had to navigate to My Events to see their new event — no affordance on the Home screen.

Fix: All event cards made tappable across every screen.

Issue 2

"Vibe" field label confused participants

Options (Quiet / Casual / Deep) were too abstract. Users couldn't interpret what selecting "Quiet" would mean for the actual dining experience.

Fix: Renamed to "Dining Atmosphere" with options: Quiet Meal / Casual Hangout / Deep Conversation.

04

Phase 04

High-Fidelity Prototype

A second round of user testing and expert critique pushed the design further. Six distinct issues were identified and addressed.

Issue found Fix applied
"Budget" vs. total cost ambiguity Renamed to Budget/Person
Group size unclear if creator counted Added hint: incl. yourself
Cancel/Edit only accessible from My Events Added buttons directly on event detail page
Chat input field below keyboard Repositioned above keyboard (standard mobile pattern)
Mute toggle had no visible feedback Replaced with pinned notice at top of chatroom
Report reason locked after selection Made reason editable before submission

04 — Evaluation

What we tested and what we found

Two rounds of in-person user testing (heuristic evaluation + think-aloud sessions) and one round of expert critique. 4–5 participants per round. No prior exposure to the prototype.

1

Round 1

Heuristic Evaluation + User Testing

Evaluated on the wireframe / medium-fidelity prototype. Each team member ran a task flow session and compiled findings using Nielsen's heuristics.

Task Issue (Heuristic violated) Recommendation
Create an event After creating, users could not tap the event card on the Home tab — had to navigate to My Events. Violates: Consistency and Standards. Made all event cards tappable, linking to the event detail page from any screen.
Create an event "Vibe" label and options (Quiet / Casual / Deep) were too abstract — users couldn't interpret their meaning. Violates: Match Between System and Real World. Renamed to "Dining Atmosphere" with options: Quiet Meal / Casual Hangout / Deep Conversation.
Find and join an event Participant avatars looked clickable but did nothing — users expected to see participant information when tapping them. Made avatars clickable to display participant profile details.
Find and join an event Search interaction was unclear — keyboard did not appear automatically when users tapped the search bar. Keyboard now appears immediately when the search bar is tapped.
Communicate in chatroom Toggling "Mute Notifications" had no visible change in the chatroom interface. Violates: Visibility of System Status and User Control and Freedom. Added a pinned notice at the top of the chatroom showing key event info (meeting time, location) for all participants.
Login & manage profile Error message on failed login was not visually prominent — easy to overlook. Violates: Visibility of System Status. Redesigned error message with stronger contrast and clearer placement.
2

Round 2

Heuristic Evaluation + User Testing

Evaluated on the high-fidelity prototype. Heuristic evaluation surfaced structural issues, followed by think-aloud user testing with 4–5 participants across all four task flows.

Heuristic Evaluation

Task Issue Recommendation
Task Issue Recommendation
Cancel and Edit Event — from event detail page Users who accessed an event detail page from the Home screen had no way to cancel or edit — they had to go to My Events first. Limits flexibility of use. Added Cancel and Edit buttons directly on the event detail page, regardless of entry point.
View Event details Only a small "›" button on the right side of an event card was tappable. Conflicts with the proximity principle — the full card should be the target. Retained "›" as a visual affordance but expanded the entire event card as the tappable area.
Communicate in chatroom — send a message Chat input field was positioned beneath the keyboard, deviating from standard mobile messaging patterns and creating an unnatural layout. Input field repositioned directly above the keyboard, matching standard mobile messaging conventions.
Newly established chatroom — edge case The design did not account for the empty state of a newly created chatroom (no messages, no participants yet) — interface felt incomplete. Added an empty chatroom state to represent real user scenarios after event creation.
Login & manage profile The Login & Security screen had no clear entry point for help or support related to account and security tasks. Added a Help & Support button directly on the Login & Security page.

User Testing

Task Issue Recommendation
Create Event — preferences screen "Budget" was ambiguous (total vs. per-person?). "Group Size" was unclear whether it includes the creator. Renamed "Budget" to "Budget/Person"; added hint "incl. yourself" to Group Size field.
Communicate in chatroom — report a user Once a report reason was selected, users couldn't modify it without restarting the entire flow. Updated so users can change their selected reason before submission, without needing to restart.
Communicate in chatroom — view user by clicking avatars Users could tap other participants' avatars to view profiles, but could NOT tap "You" to view their own profile — had to navigate away from the chatroom. Tapping "You" now opens the user's own profile preview from within the chatroom.
Login & manage profile Confirmation screens and selected states lacked visual polish — users couldn't clearly recognize when an action was completed. Redesigned confirmation screens with clearer card layout and subtle highlight background.
View Participants / View User Profile Only part of the participant list was clickable (e.g., only the first of four users). Participant avatars were missing from the list. Added avatars for all participants; made every participant in the list clickable.

16

total issues surfaced across 2 evaluation rounds

Label clarity

most recurring friction point — small wording changes had outsized impact on user confidence

Navigation consistency

users expected the same action to be available regardless of which screen they entered from

Safety features

report flow and profile previews were expected by participants even when not prompted

05 — Reflection

What we learned

What worked

A counterintuitive north star

Grounding every decision in one specific, counterintuitive research finding — conversational fit matters more than food preference — gave the team a shared reference point. Every field label and feature could be evaluated against that single principle.

What we'd do differently

Broader participant pool, earlier metrics

Our participants skewed toward Chinese international students, limiting generalizability. A more diverse sample would have surfaced different safety concerns and dining norms. We'd also introduce quantitative metrics (SUS, task completion rates) earlier in the process.

What's next

Matching, verification, empty states

A matching algorithm surfacing compatible companions based on conversational style. Verified profiles to address safety concerns. An empty-state experience for newly created events with no joiners yet.
